unit.name: DQN on Atari Breakout
unit.description: Applies the DQN formulation to Breakout, including image-based states, action-value outputs, preprocessing, and convolutional architecture.
unit.summary: Breakout is introduced as an Atari task where the agent controls a paddle, wins by destroying bricks, and loses if the ball passes the paddle [ts=3215s] [ts=3221s]. The Q-network input is the game screen and its outputs are Q-values for possible actions such as left, right, and no-op [ts=3307s] [ts=3331s]. Preprocessing reduces the visual state by cropping irrelevant regions, converting to grayscale, reducing image dimensions, and stacking four frames to encode motion [ts=3404s] [ts=3461s] [ts=3562s]. The architecture shown for DQN uses convolutional layers with ReLU followed by fully connected layers and a linear output layer that emits Q-values for each action [ts=3621s] [ts=3647s].

key_points.text: In Breakout, the goal is to destroy all bricks; the paddle controls the ball and losing occurs when the ball passes the paddle.
The DQN output for Breakout is a vector of Q-values, one for each discrete action such as left, right, or idle.
Preprocessing can remove irrelevant pixels such as the score or bottom area when they do not affect the strategy for Breakout.
Grayscale conversion and dimension reduction make the screen input cheaper while preserving task-relevant visual information.
Stacking a history of four frames lets the Q-network infer motion, such as where the ball is going.
The DQN architecture for image inputs uses convolutional layers, ReLU activations, fully connected layers, and a linear Q-value output.
